data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back in because the concept of 'severe testing' implicitly relies on the uniformity of nature: assuming that conditions which falsified rivals in the past will remain relevant or similar in the future.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If 'severity' can be defined purely logically (e.g., logical content) without reference to empirical regularities, the inductive smuggling charge fails.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the preference is viewed solely as a psychological habit of scientists rather than a normative rule, the logical contradiction dissolves.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Deconstructing 'Severity': A test is only 'severe' if the outcome was improbable given the background knowledge. This background knowledge itself rests on the assumption that natural regularities observed previously hold now. Therefore, preferring a theory based on past severe tests assumes the future will resemble the past regarding the relevance of those tests, which is the very principle of induction Popper rejected. The 'cost' of accepting this is admitting Popper's system is not purely deductive and requires a minimal, perhaps tacit, inductive postulate to function in practice.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
